en: To make a bad situation better
hook: AMELIORATE: 'meliorate' sounds like 'better' (meilleur in French). Make better.
story: Ameliorate. In the coastal village of Kalapara, children kept falling sick from the salty, dirty pond water. Then a small charity arrived. They installed tube wells, taught families to boil water, and trained one mother in every lane to recognise early symptoms. A year later, the clinic's waiting room was half empty. The situation had been ameliorated: made better. To ameliorate is to improve a bad condition. It is a favourite GRE word for policies that ease suffering.

gre.s: The new irrigation canals did much to ____ the effects of the drought, though they could not entirely prevent crop losses.
gre.clue: though they could not entirely prevent crop losses

example: Planting trees along the busy roads of Gazipur could ameliorate the summer heat for thousands of factory workers.

en: To cause someone to become hostile or annoyed
bn: বিরূপ করে তোলা; শত্রুতা সৃষ্টি করা
hook: ANTAGONIZE: turn someone into your ANTAGONIST (enemy).
story: Antagonize. Nadia's new flatmate began by borrowing her shampoo without asking. Then she played loud music at midnight, mocked Nadia's cooking in front of guests, and parked her bicycle across Nadia's door. Within a month, the once friendly Nadia would not even say hello. Her flatmate had antagonized her: caused her to become hostile and annoyed. An antagonist is an opponent, like the villain of a film. Synonyms: provoke, alienate, offend.

gre.s: Eager not to ____ the powerful landlords whose support he needed, the reformer softened his proposals until they offended no one.
gre.clue: until they offended no one

example: The referee's arrogant manner antagonized both teams, and by halftime even the home fans were jeering him.

en: The highest or most successful point; the point in an orbit farthest from Earth
hook: APO-GEE: AWAY (apo) from Earth (geo), the farthest, highest point.
story: Apogee. Tanvir's grandfather was a village jatra actor. The apogee of his career came in 1985, when he performed before ten thousand people at a festival in Dhaka. After that, the crowds slowly shrank. An apogee is the highest or most successful point. In astronomy, it is the point in the orbit of the Moon or a satellite farthest from Earth: apo means away, and gee means earth. Its opposite is perigee. Synonyms: peak, zenith, pinnacle.

gre.s: Critics agree that the novelist's career reached its ____ with her third book; nothing she wrote afterward came close to its brilliance or its success.
gre.clue: nothing she wrote afterward came close

example: Many scholars regard the reign of Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, as the apogee of Mughal architecture.

en: Humorously rude and indecent
hook: BAWDY: BAWLING out rude jokes.
story: Bawdy. At village weddings in the old days, women from the groom's side would sing teasing songs full of jokes about married life, making the bride blush and the aunties roar with laughter. The songs were bawdy: humorously rude and indecent. Bawdy humour is crude but cheerful, not cruel. Shakespeare's plays are full of bawdy puns that schoolbooks quietly skip. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: ribald, racy, risque.

gre.s: The comedian's ____ jokes, full of sexual innuendo, delighted the late-night crowd but would never have been permitted on family television.
gre.clue: full of sexual innuendo

example: Chaucer's bawdy tales of millers and cheating wives still make university students blush and laugh.

en: A large, destructive fire
hook: CONFLAGRATION: a FLAG-burning FLAME everywhere.
story: Conflagration. One night, a fire broke out in a chemical warehouse in Old Dhaka. Flames leapt from building to building through the narrow lanes, gas cylinders exploded, and firefighters battled for hours. By morning, whole blocks had turned to ash. It was a conflagration: a large, destructive fire. Con means together and flagrare means to burn, the root of flagrant. The word can also describe a war that spreads like fire. Synonyms: inferno, blaze, firestorm.

gre.s: What began as a small kitchen fire soon became a ____ that consumed half the town, as dry winds drove the flames from roof to roof.
gre.clue: consumed half the town

example: The Great Fire of London in 1666 was a conflagration that destroyed more than thirteen thousand houses.

en: Pleasant and friendly; well suited to one's taste or nature
hook: CON-GENIAL: comes with a GENIAL, friendly feeling.
story: Congenial. After two lonely months studying in her room, Mitu finally joined a GRE study group at a café in Dhanmondi. She was nervous. But the members passed her their best notes, laughed at her terrible mnemonics, and ordered an extra cup of tea for her without asking. By the end of the evening she felt she had known them for years. Congenial means pleasant, friendly, and well suited to you. A congenial place makes it easy to be yourself.

gre.s: Although the two scientists had been bitter rivals in print, they found each other surprisingly ____ in person, chatting amiably for hours.
gre.clue: chatting amiably for hours

example: Rahim found the quiet public library in Chattogram far more congenial for study than his family's noisy flat.

en: To describe or portray precisely; to mark the boundary of
bn: সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে বর্ণনা করা; সীমা নির্ধারণ করা
hook: DE-LINE-ATE: draw the LINES clearly.
story: Delineate. Before a new school was built in the village, Sabbir, a land surveyor, walked the plot with a measuring tape and drove bamboo stakes into the ground, marking exactly where the school's land ended and the farmers' fields began. He had delineated the boundary: marked it precisely. The word also means to describe precisely: a good report delineates each step of a plan. The word line is inside it, so think of drawing clear lines. Synonyms: outline, define, depict.

gre.s: Because the old treaty failed to ____ the border precisely, both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank.
gre.clue: both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank

example: The new contract clearly delineates who must pay for repairs, ending years of argument between the tenants and the owner.

en: To criticize unfairly; to belittle
hook: DENIGRATE: blacken (niger) someone's name.
story: Denigrate. At a family dinner, cousin Imran mocked Joya's decision to study fine arts. "Painting? That is not a real subject. You will end up drawing portraits at a village fair." He ignored the fact that her paintings had already won a national prize. He was denigrating her work: criticizing it unfairly and belittling it. The Latin root means to blacken, so to denigrate is to blacken someone's name. Synonyms: disparage, belittle, deprecate.

gre.s: Rather than engage with the substance of her argument, her rivals chose to ____ her credentials, dismissing her as a mere amateur despite her decades of research.
gre.clue: dismissing her as a mere amateur

example: Some nineteenth-century critics denigrated photography as a mechanical trick, unworthy of being called an art.

en: Holding total power and often using it cruelly
hook: DESPOTIC: a DESPOT, an all-powerful tyrant.
story: Despotic. In a history class, Nabil read about an ancient king who executed anyone who criticized him, seized farmers' harvests whenever he wished, and made every law himself, with no council and no court to stop him. His teacher called the king's rule despotic: absolute and often cruel. A despot is a ruler with total power. The word can describe a boss or a parent too: a despotic manager tolerates no disagreement. Synonyms: tyrannical, autocratic, dictatorial.

gre.s: The new leader, who had promised a return to democracy, soon proved just as ____ as his predecessor, jailing critics and ruling by decree.
gre.clue: jailing critics and ruling by decree

example: Under the despotic governor, newspapers were shut down and any farmer who complained about taxes risked prison.

en: A long, angry speech or piece of writing attacking someone
hook: DIATRIBE: a speech that would make a whole TRIBE DIE of embarrassment.
story: Diatribe. Uncle Jamal's phone was stolen on a crowded bus. When he got home, he did not just complain. For twenty full minutes, he raged: against the thief, the police, the bus company, the government, the traffic, and young people in general. Nobody could interrupt. When he finally stopped, his tea had gone cold. That was a diatribe: a long, bitter, angry attack in speech or writing. It is criticism with all the brakes removed.

gre.s: What began as a measured critique of the policy soon devolved into a ____ against everyone who had ever supported it.
gre.clue: What began as a measured critique

example: The retired colonel's letter to the editor was a diatribe against cyclists, whom he blamed for every traffic jam in town.

en: Amusing in a dry, odd, or whimsical way
hook: DROLL: a DOLL that makes funny, dry jokes.
story: Droll. At his ninetieth birthday party, a young relative asked Grandfather how it felt to be so old. He thought about it seriously. "Like an old car," he said, with a perfectly straight face. "Everything still works. Except the engine. And the wheels. And the brakes." The room exploded with laughter, but he did not even smile. His humour was droll: amusing in a dry, quiet, slightly odd way. Droll comedians never laugh at their own jokes.

gre.s: The memoir's ____ observations, delivered with a perfectly straight face, had readers laughing at the most mundane details of office life.
gre.clue: had readers laughing

example: The museum guide had a droll way of describing ancient tax collectors that kept the bored students giggling.

en: To fill with delight; to charm
hook: EN-CHANT: like a magical CHANT that casts a spell.
story: Enchant. Every winter, an old storyteller visits Joya's village. He sits under the banyan tree and tells tales of clever tigers, foolish kings, and flying horses, changing his voice for every character. The children sit silent for hours, eyes wide, forgetting to blink. Even the adults stop to listen. He enchants them: fills them with delight, charms them as if by magic. An enchanting smile captures every heart. Think of a magical chant.

gre.s: The village's winding lanes and flower-covered cottages never fail to ____ visitors, many of whom return year after year.
gre.clue: many of whom return year after year

example: The puppet show at Shilpakala Academy enchanted the children, who sat in complete silence for an hour.

en: To keep away from something on purpose
hook: ESCHEW: sounds like a sneeze, 'ah-CHOO!' — you avoid it.
story: Eschew. After a heart scare at fifty-five, Nadia's father changed his life overnight. No more fried singara. No more sugar in his tea. No more cigarettes. He walked five kilometres every morning, ate fish and vegetables, and politely refused every rich dish at weddings. He eschewed all the things that had nearly killed him: deliberately avoided them. Eschew even sounds like a sneeze, ah-choo, as you turn away. Good writers eschew unnecessary words.

gre.s: The minimalist architect tended to ____ ornament of any kind, preferring bare concrete and plain glass.
gre.clue: preferring bare concrete and plain glass

example: The young poet eschewed rhyme altogether, believing it made her verses sound like advertising jingles.

en: To pretend to be affected by a feeling or state
hook: FEIGN: sounds like FAKE + FAINT; fake a faint.
story: Feign. On the morning of the math test, eight-year-old Babu lay in bed clutching his stomach. "Ammu, it hurts so much!" he groaned, eyes squeezed shut. His mother felt his forehead, sighed, and said he could stay home. Ten minutes later, she found him dancing in front of the TV. He had been feigning illness: pretending to feel something he did not. Feigned interest, feigned surprise, feigned sleep. Think: fake a faint.

gre.s: Though secretly delighted by the news, the diplomat chose to ____ indifference so as not to reveal his government's hand.
gre.clue: so as not to reveal his government's hand

example: Mahin feigned surprise when his friends burst in with a cake, though he had overheard their plans a week earlier.

en: Recklessly bold or rash
hook: FOOL-HARDY: a FOOL who's too HARDY for his own good.
story: Foolhardy. During the monsoon floods, a group of young men dared each other to swim across the swollen Padma for a bet of five hundred taka. The current was strong enough to drown expert swimmers. One of them nearly did, rescued only by a passing fisherman. The stunt was foolhardy: recklessly bold, brave in a stupid way. Being intrepid is admirable; being foolhardy is dangerous. Think: a fool who is too hardy.

gre.s: Experienced mountaineers considered the attempt ____, since the climbers planned to ascend in midwinter without oxygen or guides.
gre.clue: in midwinter without oxygen or guides

example: Selling the family shop to buy cryptocurrency on a stranger's tip was a foolhardy move that Kamal deeply regretted.

en: Acting suddenly, on impulse, without thinking first
hook: IMPETUOUS: full of IMPETUS (sudden force), no brakes.
story: Impetuous. During a heated argument with his boss about a project deadline, Farhan slammed his laptop shut and shouted, "I quit!" He walked out, feeling powerful. By the evening, he felt sick. He had no savings, no other job, and a family depending on him. His decision had been impetuous: made quickly, on impulse, without careful thought. Impetus means sudden force. Impetuous people act first and think later.

gre.s: The general's ____ decision to attack before reinforcements arrived, made in a moment of anger, cost him the battle.
gre.clue: made in a moment of anger

example: In an impetuous moment, the young batsman charged down the pitch to the very first ball and was stumped.

en: Seemingly endless; tediously long
hook: IN-TERMINABLE: can't be TERMINATED.
story: Interminable. The annual general meeting of the housing society began at ten in the morning. By two in the afternoon, members were still arguing about the colour of the front gate. Rahim checked his watch, then the window, then his watch again. The meeting felt interminable: seemingly endless and tediously long. In means not, and terminus means end, as in terminal and terminate. Dhaka's traffic jams can feel interminable too. Synonyms: endless, unending, protracted.

gre.s: Audiences who had expected a brisk thriller found the film ____: its three-hour running time was padded with lengthy scenes in which almost nothing happened.
gre.clue: padded with lengthy scenes in which almost nothing happened

example: Stuck in an interminable traffic jam on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, Shirin finished an entire novel.

en: A joking attitude toward something that deserves seriousness
hook: LEVITY: LIGHT as LEVITATING.
story: Levity. At a serious faculty meeting about falling exam results, a young lecturer joked that perhaps the students were studying the wrong syllabus on purpose. A few people laughed, but the dean frowned. This was no time for levity: treating serious matters with humor or a lack of respect. Levity comes from the Latin levis, light, as in levitate; it is lightness where weight is expected. Its opposite is gravity, meaning seriousness. Synonyms: frivolity, flippancy, jocularity.

gre.s: The speaker's ____ seemed badly misjudged; his jokes about the earthquake offended an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims.
gre.clue: an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims

example: The judge warned that any further levity in the courtroom would be treated as contempt.

en: Illegal or dishonest acts by someone in an official post
hook: MAL-FEASANCE: BAD doing (mal = bad).
story: Malfeasance. A district official was given money to build tube wells in fifty villages. Two years later, auditors found only ten wells, while the official had a new house and a new car. He was charged with malfeasance: wrongdoing, especially by a public official. Mal means bad, as in malpractice and malnutrition, and feasance means doing. Compare nonfeasance, failing to do one's duty at all. Synonyms: misconduct, corruption, wrongdoing. Opposite: probity.

gre.s: Once celebrated as a reformer, the mayor left office in disgrace after an inquiry uncovered years of ____, including bribery and the theft of public funds.
gre.clue: including bribery and the theft of public funds

example: Investigators found evidence of malfeasance at the port authority, where officials had been taking bribes to release cargo uninspected.

en: To speak harmful untruths about someone (verb); evil or harmful (adjective)
hook: MAL = bad. To say bad things about someone.
story: Malign. Jealous of her success, a rival shop owner began spreading rumours about Rahima. He told customers that she sold expired medicine and cheated on her taxes. None of it was true. Slowly, people stopped visiting her pharmacy. He had maligned her: spoken harmful untruths to damage her reputation. As an adjective, malign means evil or harmful, the opposite of benign. Mal means bad, as in malfunction and malice.

gre.s: Although tabloids continue to ____ the senator as corrupt, every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper.
gre.clue: every investigation into her finances has found nothing improper

example: Anonymous accounts maligned the young cricketer online, falsely claiming that he had taken money to lose matches.

en: Former
hook: ONETIME: ONE TIME in the past.
story: Onetime. At a cricket coaching camp in Khulna, the boys noticed an old man quietly correcting their batting stances. Someone whispered that he was a onetime national team opener, famous back in the nineteen eighties. Onetime means former: what someone used to be. A onetime rival can become a friend; a onetime jute mill can become a shopping centre. Do not confuse it with one-time, meaning happening only once. Synonyms: former, erstwhile, previous.

gre.s: The senator, a ____ ally of the president, has become one of his fiercest critics since their bitter public quarrel over the budget last year.
gre.clue: has become one of his fiercest critics

example: Sabina, a onetime nurse, now runs a small bakery in Uttara that is famous for its mango cakes.

en: A person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts
hook: PHILISTINE: thinks a museum is a waste of land.
story: Philistine. When the town council planned to demolish a two-hundred-year-old zamindar palace to build a parking lot, Ishita protested. One councillor shrugged: 'Old buildings, paintings, poetry, what use are they? They make no money.' Ishita called him a philistine: a person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts. The name comes from an ancient people portrayed in the Bible as enemies of the Israelites. Opposite: aesthete. Synonyms: boor, barbarian.

gre.s: Dismissing the museum as a waste of public money, the mayor revealed himself to be a ____, indifferent to the paintings and sculptures that had made the city famous.
gre.clue: indifferent to the paintings and sculptures

example: Only a philistine would cover the wall of a centuries-old terracotta temple with advertising posters.

en: Slow, heavy, and monotonous; working steadily but without inspiration
hook: PLODDING: the PLOD-PLOD sound of tired, heavy footsteps.
story: Plodding. Every morning, an old buffalo pulls a wooden cart down the road past Imran's school. Slow, heavy step after slow, heavy step, never faster, never stopping. Rickshaws overtake it; children overtake it; even a tortoise might. Later that day, Imran's film critic friend reviewed a new movie: "A plodding three-hour story." Plodding means slow, heavy, and monotonous. It can also describe someone who works steadily but without inspiration or brilliance.

gre.s: Critics praised the film's acting but found its ____ pace exhausting, as scenes dragged on long after their point had been made.
gre.clue: scenes dragged on long after their point had been made

example: The biography's plodding chapters on tax records nearly made me give up before reaching the exciting war years.

en: Dangerously steep; sudden and dramatic
hook: PRECIPITOUS: like a PRECIPICE, a sheer cliff.
story: Precipitous. The road to Sajek Valley climbs through the hills with precipitous drops on one side: almost vertical slopes falling away into the forest far below. Lamia gripped the jeep's railing and refused to look down. Precipitous means dangerously steep. It also means sudden and dramatic, as in a precipitous fall in prices. Think of a precipice, the edge of a cliff. Related is precipitate, meaning hasty or rash. Synonyms: steep, sheer, abrupt. Its opposite is gradual.

gre.s: The company's decline was ____: in a single quarter, its share price fell by ninety percent, wiping out a decade of steady growth.
gre.clue: in a single quarter

example: After the mill closed, the town's population suffered a precipitous fall, from forty thousand to barely ten thousand.

en: Ordinary and dull; lacking imagination
hook: PROSAIC: like plain PROSE, not poetry.
story: Prosaic. Standing on the bank of the Padma at sunset, Lamia's friend whispered, "Look. Golden fire melting into silver water." Lamia looked. "It is nice," she said. "It is orange." Her friend laughed: "You are so prosaic!" Prosaic means ordinary and unimaginative, like plain prose compared with poetry. The prosaic details of daily life include bills, groceries, and laundry. Prosaic is not wrong; it is just without magic.

gre.s: Fans expecting a dramatic explanation for the band's breakup were disappointed by the ____ truth: the members had simply grown tired of touring.
gre.clue: had simply grown tired of touring

example: The famous painter's daily routine turned out to be prosaic, with breakfast at seven, work until noon, and an afternoon nap.

en: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
hook: QUANDARY: 'QUAND?' (when?) and 'where?' — totally stuck.
story: Quandary. Two job offers reached Nadia on the same day. One was in Dhaka, close to her ailing mother, with a modest salary. The other was in Singapore, with double the pay and a real chance to build a career. She paced the hostel corridor all night, unable to decide. She was in a quandary: a state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation. A quandary is close to a dilemma. Synonyms: dilemma, predicament, plight.

gre.s: The doctor faced a genuine ____: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate her duty of honesty.
gre.clue: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate

example: The referee faced a quandary when the floodlights failed with the scores level and only two minutes left to play.

en: To damage or destroy something badly over a wide area
hook: RAVAGE: like a RAVENOUS SAVAGE destroying everything.
story: Ravage. In 2007, Cyclone Sidr struck the southwest coast of Bangladesh. Winds tore roofs from houses, the storm surge swept away fields and livestock, and whole villages were flattened. Cyclones like this ravage the coast: they cause severe and extensive damage. The ravages of time, war or disease are their destructive effects. Do not confuse ravage with ravish, which means to seize or enrapture. Synonyms: devastate, destroy, wreck.

gre.s: Unless farmers act quickly to control the locusts, the swarms will ____ the region's crops, leaving little to harvest and threatening famine.
gre.clue: leaving little to harvest

example: Years of civil war had ravaged the country's roads, so aid trucks needed four days to cover two hundred kilometres.

en: Making a show of being morally superior to others
hook: SANCTIMONIOUS: acts like a SAINT, but it's all for MONEY and show.
story: Sanctimonious. At every press conference, the politician lectured citizens about honesty, family values, and serving the nation with clean hands. He quoted holy books and wagged his finger at the camera. Then journalists discovered that he had taken bribes for twenty years and owned four secret flats abroad. His speeches had been sanctimonious: making a show of being morally superior to others. Holier-than-thou is a close synonym.

gre.s: Voters grew tired of the senator's ____ speeches about honesty, particularly after he was caught concealing his own debts.
gre.clue: after he was caught concealing his own debts

example: My cousin's sanctimonious posts about healthy eating would be easier to bear if he did not eat fuchka every evening.

en: Very careful to do what is right; extremely attentive to detail
hook: SCRUPULOUS: has SCRUPLES, a moral conscience.
story: Scrupulous. At the supermarket, the cashier accidentally gave Arif five hundred taka too much in change. He noticed only when he was three blocks away. It was raining. He walked back anyway, soaked, and returned the money to the astonished cashier. Arif is scrupulous: careful to always do what is right. Scrupulous also means extremely careful about details, as in scrupulous research. The opposite, unscrupulous, means dishonest and without morals.

gre.s: The biographer was ____ about sources, refusing to include any anecdote that she could not verify with at least two documents.
gre.clue: refusing to include any anecdote that she could not verify

example: Scrupulous record keeping let the laboratory trace every blood sample back to the exact patient and hour.

en: Serious, respectable, and unadventurous
hook: STAID: STAYED the same forever, never adventurous.
story: Staid. Every Friday for thirty years, Kamal's uncle has worn the same grey shirt, read the same newspaper, and eaten lunch at the same restaurant in Old Dhaka, always ordering the same kacchi biriyani. He distrusts jokes, loud colours, and new ideas. He is staid: serious, respectable, and unadventurous. Staid is an old spelling of stayed, as if fixed in place. A staid newspaper has a dignified, conservative style. Opposite: flamboyant. Synonyms: sedate, sober, conservative.

gre.s: Once known for its ____ coverage of parliamentary procedure, the newspaper has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip.
gre.clue: has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip

example: The staid old bank surprised its customers by hiring a rapper to star in its new advertising campaign.
